description: ARA turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar into a people-first map of the Amazon. In 2023-24 the Rio Negro hit its lowest levels in 123 years, cutting riverside towns off. NISAR sees through clouds and the forest canopy: we map water, flooded forest and burn scars on 19 dates, validated against Sentinel-2 (F1 0.89), and show who is affected. With El Niño data and machine learning we forecast droughts 3 months ahead. Skills: Python, SAR/satellite data, ML and web maps. Open code, open science.
summary:
Ara turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar into a people-first map of the Amazon's water, fire and power. In 2023 and 2024 the Rio Negro at Manaus hit its two lowest levels in 123 years, cutting riverside towns off from food, medicine and the diesel that powers them, while clouds and smoke blinded optical satellites. NISAR's L-band radar sees through both and even detects water under the forest canopy.

We read 19 NISAR dates around Manaus and Tefé (only 150-220 MB of each multi-gigabyte file), validated the water map against ESA Sentinel-2 (F1 0.89) and combined it with population, NASA FIRMS fires, NASA POWER, river gauges and hydropower data. Every view leads with the people affected: 194,000 living by the water in June, 112,000 by November. El Niño is linked only where our data support it: the river bottoms out about 3 m lower after strong El Niños than after strong La Niñas.

A 3-month river forecast, a fire-and-smoke nowcast and an energy view help civil defense, health and energy planners act months before the river closes. All code is open for others to reuse.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Ara is an interactive web map showing how the Amazon's yearly flood-and-drought pulse, and its disruption by El Niño, reaches people. Four views each open with the number of people affected:

- Rivers: NISAR radar maps of open water and flooded forest (water under the canopy) on 19 dates, June-November 2026. Around Manaus, 97% of the flooded forest drained and the people living by the water fell from 194,000 to 112,000.

- Fire: NASA FIRMS fires, people within 3 km of a fire (337,000) and burn scars detected by the radar itself: 222 patches, 92% confirmed by fire satellites vs 12% for random forest points.

- Fire now: fires of the last 48 h, fire weather and wind for the next 72 h, smoke sectors and the people in the smoke path (57,000).

- Energy: five hydropower plants (river inflow vs normal, output), solar potential under smoke, and the risk that a severe drought stops the diesel barges that power isolated towns. Balbina, the reservoir serving Manaus, is at 30% of its normal inflow.

How it works: each NISAR file is 2-13 GB, so we open it remotely and read only the radar bands over the study area (150-220 MB, about 2 minutes per date on a laptop). Frames are mosaicked at 100 m; water, flooded forest (double bounce) and urban areas are classified for each pass, and areas no pass covered are shown hatched, never guessed. The water map is validated against ESA Sentinel-2 on every date (F1 0.89 Manaus, 0.84 Tefé). WorldPop population is crossed with water, fires and smoke. Gradient-boosted quantile models forecast river level, rainfall and fire 1-6 months ahead from the El Niño index (3-month river skill +0.25 over climatology).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Decision support: civil defense and health agencies can pre-position water, food, medicine and fuel months ahead and know which square kilometers and how many people to reach first; fire brigades can rank fires by fire weather and people downwind; energy planners can watch reservoir inflow and diesel-route risk.

- Open science: open code and data, a checksum for every NISAR file used, and a reproducible recipe that makes NISAR usable without a supercomputer. Any Amazon town can be added in about 30 minutes of processing.

- Our goal: early warnings for riverside communities and partnerships with civil defense and research institutions.

TOOLS

Python (numpy, pandas, rasterio, h5py, scipy, scikit-learn, shapely, asf_search, matplotlib, Pillow); JavaScript with Vite, deck.gl, MapLibre and Chart.js; GitHub Pages and Docker. Data: NASA-ISRO NISAR, NASA FIRMS, NASA POWER, SRTM, ESA Sentinel-2 and WorldCover, NOAA ONI, WorldPop, ANA river gauge and ONS hydropower.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- People first: every view starts with who is affected, not with pixels.

- NISAR on a laptop: partial remote reads cut each file to about 1/20.

- The radar checks itself: it finds burn scars that fire satellites confirm, and fills the gap when clouds and smoke blind optical images.

- A guided 5-step story, a click-for-definition glossary and a map you can click to see who lives in each square kilometer.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty: every El Niño claim carries an evidence label (strong, clear in strong events or indirect); fire follows drought reaching the river more than the Pacific index alone.

- Validation and limits: we report where optical references fail and show coverage gaps instead of filling them.

- Accessibility: plain language, mobile layout and open data with no login.

- Use of AI: built with an AI coding assistant under our direction, disclosed in the repository.
